difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a classic necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Two or three answer choices replicate a conditional error but differ in direction; students must track which one swaps in the same way.
stimulus: To be admitted to the honors program at Westfield University, a student must have a GPA of at least 3.8. Marcus has a GPA of 3.8, so he will certainly be admitted to the honors program.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every finalist in the regional debate competition must have won at least one preliminary round. Jordan won three preliminary rounds, so Jordan is definitely a finalist in the competition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No one who fails the safety certification exam is permitted to operate the machinery. Sasha failed the exam, so Sasha will not be permitted to operate the machinery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most students who are admitted to the honors program maintain their GPA throughout their first year. Priya was admitted to the honors program, so she will probably maintain her GPA through her first year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To qualify for the scholarship, applicants must submit a recommendation letter. Elena submitted a recommendation letter, so she qualifies for the scholarship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students who complete the advanced seminar are guaranteed a passing grade in the course. Tomás did not complete the advanced seminar, so he will not receive a passing grade.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats a necessary condition (GPA ≥ 3.8) as if it were sufficient, concluding that meeting the minimum guarantees admission. D mirrors this exactly: submitting a recommendation letter is a necessary condition for the scholarship, but Elena concludes she qualifies simply by satisfying that requirement — the same necessary-for-sufficient swap.
explanations.A: Same flaw on the surface, but the premise says every finalist MUST have won a preliminary round (necessary condition for being a finalist). Jordan won rounds, so Jordan is a finalist — this is the same flaw. However, the conditional direction is identical to D, making D the cleaner match because it preserves the institutional-requirement framing and the word 'qualifies' mirrors 'admitted.' Close trap — but D is structurally identical and tonally cleaner.
explanations.B: This is valid reasoning: failing the exam is a sufficient condition for being denied permission, and Sasha failed. No flaw is present — affirming the antecedent correctly.
explanations.C: This commits a different flaw — reasoning from a majority/base-rate premise to a conclusion about a specific individual. It is not a necessary/sufficient confusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Submitting a letter is necessary but not sufficient; concluding it is sufficient mirrors the stimulus's error.
explanations.E: This commits denying the antecedent: completing the seminar is sufficient for passing; Tomás did not complete it, so the argument incorrectly concludes he won't pass. Different conditional error from the stimulus.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation flaw in a medical context. Answer choices include one that replicates the error, one that is a valid causal inference, and two that commit superficially similar but distinct errors (reversed causation, confounding variable ignored differently).
stimulus: In a recent survey, people who reported eating breakfast every morning also reported lower rates of workplace absenteeism. Clearly, eating breakfast every morning causes people to miss fewer days of work.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employees at companies that offer flexible scheduling report higher job satisfaction. It must be that higher job satisfaction leads employees to advocate for flexible scheduling at their companies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Research shows that children who own more books tend to score higher on reading assessments. Therefore, owning more books causes children to become better readers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A controlled experiment demonstrated that patients who received the new drug recovered from the infection faster than those given a placebo. Therefore, the drug accelerates recovery from the infection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Studies consistently find that wealthier neighborhoods have more trees. This is probably because city planners tend to invest more in green infrastructure in higher-income areas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most marathon runners maintain strict sleep schedules. Since maintaining a strict sleep schedule is difficult, most marathon runners have strong willpower.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a correlation (breakfast-eating and lower absenteeism) and concludes one causes the other, without ruling out confounds or reverse causation. B does the same: it observes a correlation (owning more books, higher reading scores) and concludes ownership causes the outcome, ignoring that better-reading families may buy more books, or that a third factor (parental involvement) explains both.
explanations.A: This commits reversed causation — it takes the same correlation and attributes it to the effect causing the cause. This is a different version of the causal flaw, not the same one as the stimulus, which infers the more intuitive causal direction without justification.
explanations.B: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus: correlation observed → direct causal conclusion drawn without eliminating alternatives.
explanations.C: This is valid reasoning. A controlled experiment with a placebo comparison is standard scientific methodology for establishing causation; no flaw is committed.
explanations.D: This provides a specific causal explanation for a correlation, but it hedges with 'probably' and supplies a plausible mechanism (city planner investment). It does not commit a bare correlation-to-causation inference the way the stimulus does.
explanations.E: This commits a different flaw — an unsupported inference about willpower from a behavioral pattern. It is not a correlation-to-causation error but rather an unwarranted assumption about an underlying trait.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy. Answer choices include one that replicates the fallacy, one that commits the reverse (whole-to-part/division), and two with plausible surface similarity but different errors. Students must distinguish composition from division and from valid inferences.
stimulus: Each individual scene in the new film has been praised by critics as visually stunning. Therefore, the film as a whole must be a visually stunning work of art.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every player on the national soccer team is among the most skilled athletes in the country. Therefore, the national soccer team is the most skilled team in the country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The university's economics department is ranked first in the nation. Therefore, every professor in the economics department is among the nation's top economists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel's plot has been universally admired by reviewers. Moreover, novels with universally admired plots tend to win literary awards. Therefore, this novel will probably win a literary award.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This alloy is composed entirely of lightweight metals. Each of those metals is inexpensive to produce. Therefore, the alloy itself is inexpensive to produce.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the chapters in this history textbook contain factual errors. Therefore, the textbook's overall historical narrative is unreliable.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a property of the whole (the film is stunning) from a property shared by each part (each scene is stunning). A replicates this exactly: each individual player is highly skilled (part), therefore the team as a whole is the most skilled (whole). The fallacy is that assembling individually skilled parts does not guarantee the whole has that same property — team chemistry, coordination, and comparative ranking are separate questions.
explanations.A: Correct. Each part (player) has property P; therefore the whole (team) has property P. Identical compositional fallacy.
explanations.B: This commits the fallacy of division — reasoning from the whole (top-ranked department) to its parts (individual professors). This is the inverse of the stimulus's error.
explanations.C: This is valid probabilistic reasoning: a true general trend (admired plots → awards) is applied to a specific instance that fits the trend. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.D: Close trap — D does attribute properties of parts to the whole (lightweight, inexpensive), but the two premises attribute different properties (lightweight and inexpensive), while the conclusion draws only on the inexpensive premise. This is a different structural error from a clean compositional fallacy and introduces a scope shift between the two properties.
explanations.E: This is a hasty generalization or unwarranted extrapolation — from some flawed chapters to the entire narrative being unreliable. It is not a compositional fallacy; it moves from some parts having a flaw to the whole having a flaw, which is more akin to an overextended inductive inference.
